items.text: Using the optimized standard mapping as a starting point, a randomized delayed intervention separates IGCIP gains from maturation/practice, providing evidence for individualized programming in children.
Comparing children's spectral, temporal, and spectrotemporal processing to study auditory mechanisms and electrode-interface associations that differ from adults.
Linking audition, PA, language, reading, and subclinical speech changes; even if the average intervention effect is zero, individual changes and alternative pathways can still yield insights.

Randomization identifies the overall effect of the programming protocol but does not automatically identify electrode overlap, frequency reallocation, or developmental mediation mechanisms; there is no untreated control after 12 months, and practical blinding faces challenges.

Power of 30 per arm targets large effects, and N60 is insufficient to confirm complex multiple pathways; PA/language are measured only annually, and early auditory changes do not equate to developmental data at the same frequency.

Non-random missingness cannot be solved by bootstrap; dropout without mapping changes/reversion to old mapping must be consistent with ITT commitments; recruitment retention and fixed two-year follow-up affect the actual analyzable sample.
